Good, I've got what I need. Here's the plan for the two sessions this week.

## What the course backs, applied to this client

**Why the deload is actually the right window for this.** REVL's week-7 deload strips strength load (~40–50% on the main lifts) but keeps metabolic volume high — it's a *strength* deload, not a whole-body one. That combination (light load, low neural cost, but the client isn't fried) is exactly the window the course's own progression logic wants for corrective work: bodyweight → free weight and **bilateral → unilateral** is the built-in progression sequence (Ch 2, Page 19), and single-leg drills "impart more stress on the body than double-leg drills" (Ch 11, Page 35/Table 11-12) — so you don't want to be adding that stress in Build or Peak. Deload week is the cheapest time all block to load it up. *(Applied from the course — revl-class-integration.md §4 confirms this window's neural headroom is "strength-only" but real.)*

**Assess before you correct.** The course has a purpose-built tool for exactly her complaint: the **Single-Leg Step-Up Assessment** (Ch 10, Table 10-17, Page 48–50) — it screens for asymmetric lower-extremity mobility/stability leg-to-leg, and flags likely overactive/underactive muscle groups per side (e.g., ankle collapsing inward → overactive medial gastroc/peroneals vs. underactive glute medius). Session 1 is the right place to run it — it's a movement screen, not a max-effort test, so it fits inside a deload. Note it's non-fatiguing and quick.

The Y Balance Test (Ch 10, Table 10-10/p25) is the other course tool that directly measures leg-to-leg asymmetry and ties it to injury risk — but it's flagged for athletic populations and isn't appropriate for older adults or clients with balance impairments, so use it only if she fits that profile.

## Session 1 (deload) — Assess + expose

1. **Single-leg step-up assessment**, both legs, video or eyes-on. Compare compensations side to side (foot collapse, knee valgus, hip hike, trunk lean, top-of-motion control on the descent). This is your evidence base for what "right leg does more work" actually means mechanically — write down which side breaks down and how.
2. Light **unilateral movement-pattern work** at Functional/Movement-phase intensity (bodyweight or very light load per the Ch 2 progression) — split squat, step-up, single-leg RDL — loaded conservatively on both legs, weak side first while it's freshest, matched reps not matched effort (i.e., don't chase symmetry by fatiguing the strong leg to match the weak one).
3. Keep everything else genuinely light — this is REVL's one deload week; don't turn your session into the added volume that same week is a poor window for (revl-class-integration.md §4).

## Session 2 (deload) — Reinforce + bias volume to the weak leg

1. Re-check 1–2 of the worst compensations from session 1 as a mini-retest — cheap, tells you if cueing stuck.
2. Program **unilateral accessory bias**: e.g., 3 sets each side of split squat/step-up/single-leg RDL, but the weak leg gets an extra set or the last set on strong leg is dropped — asymmetric dosing is how you actually close a strength gap, not equal sets each side.
3. Address whatever the step-up screen flagged directly — if it's a stability/control fault (e.g., glute medius underactivity, ankle stability), add a targeted low-load drill (single-leg balance, lateral band walk, controlled step-down) rather than just more loaded unilateral squatting.

## One caution, in scope-of-practice terms

If the asymmetry looks pain-driven, or the screen shows a marked, consistent one-sided breakdown that looks like an unresolved injury (not just a strength/motor-control gap), that's a physical-therapy referral, not a programming fix — the course draws that line clearly (Ch 1 scope). Ask her directly whether there's pain or a history (old injury, surgery) behind the weak leg before you proceed past the screen.

rows.response:
## Why the arms stopped growing

Two course-supported violations are very likely driving this, and they compound each other.

**1. Frequency is probably too high for recovery, not too low.** The course is explicit: resistance training frequency is *"2–3 days a week, 48–72 h rest between sessions"* per muscle group, and frequency is *inversely related to volume and intensity* — the more you tax a muscle, the more rest it needs before you hit it again *(Week 07 Ch11, p11)*. If all 4 sessions/week train biceps and triceps directly, those tissues may be getting re-loaded before they've recovered from the last bout. Training through inadequate recovery for months doesn't produce more growth — it produces stagnation, because remodeling never completes before the next stimulus arrives.

**2. No progression or periodization = diminishing returns is expected, not a mystery.** The course's own training principles say improvement requires **progression** (double-progressive protocol) and **overload** (~5% load increments), and warns that *"rate of development decreases with training"* — **diminishing returns** — the longer you run the same stimulus (*Week 07 Ch11, p7–8*). Six months on the same split with the same exercises/loads is exactly the scenario the course describes as producing a plateau. If there's no log showing systematic load/rep increases, that's the first thing to fix — it's often the real driver, not the exercise selection.

**3. Exercise Selection & Order guidance is likely being skipped.** The course's own resistance-training template calls for **multi-joint exercises before single-joint**, and Table 11-10's "Type" column specifies **multi-joint work for all adults, with single-joint after** *(Week 07 Ch11, p12–13, p29–31)*. Pure arm programs tend to be 100% single-joint isolation (curls, extensions) with no multi-joint anchor — which caps how much load and total stimulus the tissue actually receives, even before we get to leg training.

*General knowledge, not course-based:* skipping compound lower-body/back/chest work does remove a systemic anabolic stimulus that indirectly supports arm growth. I'm not going to push that — the client has made their choice, and the fix below works within it — but it's worth being transparent that it's a real trade-off, not a non-factor.

## Redesign — 4 days/week, arms only, frequency-compliant

To fix (1) without dropping to 2 days/week, split biceps-emphasis and triceps-emphasis across the week so **each muscle group is only hit twice**, not four times, with 48–72h between same-muscle sessions:

| Day | Focus | Example anchor lift | Volume style |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | Triceps-dominant | Close-grip bench press or weighted dips (multi-joint: elbow+shoulder) | Heavy: 3–5 × 6–8 @ ~80% |
| Tue | Biceps-dominant | Weighted chin-ups or inverted curls (multi-joint) | Heavy: 3–5 × 6–8 @ ~80% |
| Thu | Triceps-dominant | Different angle (overhead extension, rope pushdown) | Volume: 3–4 × 10–12 @ ~70% |
| Fri | Biceps-dominant | Different angle (incline curl, hammer curl) | Volume: 3–4 × 10–12 @ ~70% |

- Mon→Thu and Tue→Fri = 72h between sessions for the same muscle group, satisfying the frequency rule.
- Multi-joint lift first each day per exercise order guidance *(p13)*, isolation work after.
- Heavy day / volume day within the week gives you a built-in **undulating periodization** instead of the flat, unvarying stimulus that's been running for 6 months *(periodization, Ch11 p42–46)*.
- Apply **double progression**: work to the top of the rep range at a given load, then add ~5% and drop back to the bottom *(p7, p20)*. If they're hitting 2+ reps over target for 2 sessions running, that's the trigger to add load (**2-for-2 rule**).
- Every 6–8 weeks, run a deload/assessment week (lighter loads, re-test top sets) rather than grinding the same numbers indefinitely — this mirrors the course's periodization example, which closes each block with a goal-assessment week *(p45)*.

**What I still need to give you a precise fix rather than a template:** their current exercise list, working loads/reps, and whether they've been logging and intentionally adding weight over the 6 months, or repeating the same numbers. If you want, give me the client's name and I'll pull this into a proper plan file with the full reasoning chain and CSV.

Short version: **don't add heavy lifting on top of REVL Peak Week 1 — this is the single worst week in the 13-week block to do that.** Here's the reasoning and what to do instead.

## Why Peak Week 1 blocks a straight "add 2 heavy days"

**[Observed/Pattern]** REVL's Peak phase (wks 8–10) is the block's heavy wave — main lifts to ~90–95% 1RM, rest protected (:45+), and it delivers the **highest sustained neural demand** of the whole cycle. Neural headroom for outside PT work in this phase is rated **minimal**, and the skill's explicit rule for Peak is:

> "**Added PT strength dose: none additive** — support work only (activation, one light technique primer, recovery), **unless** the PT work *replaces* a REVL strength day." (`revl-class-integration.md` §12)

Stacking a second heavy strength stimulus on top of REVL's own peak = two concurrent near-maximal neural exposures in the same week — exactly the "never stack two strength peaks" trap the skill calls out (§10, §16.6).

Two more things make this week worse than usual to add load to:
- **Next week (Peak Wk 2) is REVL's own 1RM/3RM testing week** — the highest-stakes week in the block. Anything load-bearing this week directly compromises that test.
- **Running 3x/week** is a stressor REVL's own data doesn't capture at all — it adds lower-body/impact and aerobic fatigue on top of a block where "no phase leaves the lower body unloaded" (barbell hinge is on 100% of REVL Mondays, squat/hinge patterns show up in the conditioning days too). That's now three concurrent stress sources (REVL Peak + running + proposed heavy lifting) — not two.

## On "unusually good recovery, never injured"

Good to know, but the skill is explicit that **self-reported freshness is not by itself a reason to add work** — it should be verified (actual sleep, sessions attended, loads used, recent performance) rather than taken as a green light, and REVL attendance/self-report is **not medical clearance**. Run your normal ACSM/PAR-Q+ screen regardless of how he feels (Wk04 Ch5 — scope requirement, unaffected by REVL membership).

## What I'd actually do

1. **This week (Peak Wk 1) and next (Peak Wk 2 — testing):** no added heavy work. If you train him at all, keep it to activation/technique at light load, mobility, recovery work — protect the test. Ask which lift(s) REVL tests (deadlift + push press/jerk, per the block's own testing menu) and **capture those numbers** — you'll want them.
2. **Peak Wk 3** is REVL's conditioning-baseline week — same rule, protect it, don't add.
3. **Rebuild (wks 11–13)** is the right entry point for the twice-weekly heavy lifting he wants. Two reasons: it's a low-headroom-to-high-headroom phase (like Volume), and you can **anchor the block to the maxes REVL just tested in Peak Wk 2** — no re-testing needed (§3, evidence-quality note).
4. **Frequency:** given he's also running 3x/week and doing full REVL, the **Masters 2-day variant** (60–70% anchor day, gentler top end ~2×2 @ 95–100%, estimated 1RM from a rep-max rather than a true single) is the variant that actually fits — the skill notes the 4-day/3-day variants "rarely fit alongside full REVL participation." Place the two heavy days ~72h apart and away from REVL's own hinge/squat days (Monday and Wednesday) and away from his running days.
5. **Before committing to the protocol**, run the eligibility gate (medical clearance, experienced lifter, movement screen, no contraindications, barbell access, and — critically — **G6: recovery context assessed for REVL + running + the lifting combined**, not lifting alone).

If you want, tell me: which lifts he wants to peak, what his running actually looks like (days/volume/intensity), and whether he's on REVL's Perform or Move track — and I can lay out the actual Rebuild-phase week (or start a client file for him if you want this tracked properly).

Good news on this one: the "machines-only" constraint is less limiting for "more athletic" than it sounds. Here's the approach and the reasoning behind it.

**Why machines don't block athleticism**
The course's Resistance FITT-VP type guidance explicitly allows "any equipment/bodyweight" *(Table 11-10, Wk07 Ch11 p29–31)*, and the progression continuum lists **bodyweight → machine → free weight** as a legitimate sequence, not machines-as-consolation-prize *(Ch11 p19–20)*. More importantly: the qualities that actually build "athletic" — power, speed, agility, quickness, plyometric ability — sit in the course's **Load/Speed phase** and are trained via plyometrics and SAQ drills *(Ch11 p33–41)*, which are bodyweight/floor-based, not barbell-based. So her free-weight aversion isn't actually a bottleneck for the athleticism goal — *course-supported*.

**IFT phase**
At 2 years training with good recovery, she's a plausible candidate for **Load/Speed** *(Wk02 Ch2 p10–14)* — but that phase assumes movement competency established in Movement phase. Worth a quick movement screen (bend-and-lift, single-leg, push, pull, rotation — Ch10 p45–59) before assuming this; sometimes free-weight avoidance tracks with an unresolved stability/confidence gap rather than pure preference. *Applied from course.*

**Structure — 3 full-body days** (frequency 2–3×/wk per muscle group, 48–72h spacing, Ch11 p11; full-body maximizes pattern frequency on only 3 days):

1. **Warm-up** — dynamic, Functional/Movement-phase drills (Ch11 p18).
2. **Power/SAQ/plyo first** (fresh CNS — exercise order rule, Ch11 p13): jump variations, agility ladder/cone work. No equipment needed, so the machines-only constraint never touches this block. Dose conservatively at first — beginner plyo volume is 80–100 foot contacts/session (Table 11-13) — since 2 years of machine-based lifting doesn't tell you her plyo tolerance.
3. **Strength base via machines**, covering all 5 primary movement patterns (Ch2 p12): leg press/hack squat (bend-and-lift), single-leg leg press or step-up variant (single-leg), chest press (push), seated row/lat pulldown (pull), rotary torso or cable rotation (rotation — the hardest pattern to load purely on pin-loaded machines; a rotary-torso machine or cable-stack works, note this as a gap to watch). Sets/reps per Table 9-12: alternate a hypertrophy-leaning session (3–6×6–12 @ 67–85% 1RM) with a strength-leaning session (2–6×≤6 @ ≥85%) across the week — both bands are course-supported for an intermediate lifter.
4. **Conditioning finisher** — cardio machine intervals (bike, rower, stair climber) using the three-zone model (Table 8-11) for the "engine" component of athleticism.
5. **Cool-down/flexibility** (Table 11-7).

**Progression**: double progression / 2-for-2 rule, ~5% load increments (Ch11 p7, p20). Since she's past novice, periodize if you're working toward a specific horizon (Ch11 p42–46) — otherwise undulate the hypertrophy/strength split week to week.

**On the intimidation itself** — this is a rapport/behavior-change matter, not a training-variable one *(general knowledge, Ch3/4 territory)*. I'd let machines carry the load-bearing strength work indefinitely and only reintroduce free weights later if *she* raises it, since nothing in the athleticism goal actually requires them.

If you want, give me her name and I'll build this out as a full plan with sets/reps/progression tracked in her files — I'd just need a few intake items first (recent injuries, current baseline lifts/times if any, plyo/sprint experience, session length).

## Reading the case

This is REVL + PT integration (`revl-class-integration.md`) crossed with a fatigue/recovery problem, not a stimulus problem. A few things line up:

- **Rebuild (wk 11–13)** is a moderate-headroom phase — RPE/RIR-based, "as Volume" for PT dosing (§4, §14). So the phase itself isn't why they're wrecked.
- **"Destroyed every week"** is a fatigue marker, not a training-goal statement. The course's MODIFY sequence for soreness/poor sleep/fatigue/reduced performance applies before you touch programming at all (§15): drop intensity → drop volume → swap to a lower-demand variant → change session type entirely → if it persists beyond ~1 week, reduce total load, **scale REVL itself**, review sleep/stress, and refer out if unresolved *(recovery & overtraining, Wk07 Ch11 p47–48; scope Wk01 Ch1 p7–8)*.
- **6 h sleep + moderate work stress** is a recovery-context flag, not a training-variable one. The course's Recovery FITT (frequency/time/type/intensity of recovery, Ch11 p47–48) is thin here — it doesn't give sleep thresholds, so I'm not going to invent one. **General knowledge, flagged as such:** chronically under-recovering on 6 h sleep blunts the muscle-protein-synthesis and CNS-recovery response training depends on — it's a legitimate reason to reduce *stress*, not chase more stimulus, even though the goal is size.

**The trap to avoid:** "wants size" does not mean "add more volume." REVL already saturates compound/lower-body/axial exposure every week (hinge 51% of all sessions, squat 28%, no day leaves the lower body unloaded — §5a, §6). Adding hypertrophy "more of the same" on top of a client who already feels destroyed is the fastest way to make it worse.

## What actually moves the needle here

**1. The one PT session — smallest effective dose, targeted, not generic (§14 "build muscle" row + §6a gaps).**
Compound volume is already covered by REVL. What's missing is targeted, controlled, tissue-specific hypertrophy work on under-served tissue: horizontal pull, upper back, arms, rear delts, calves. Hypertrophy band from Table 9-12 *(Wk07 Ch11 p16)*: 3–6 sets × 6–12 reps, 30–90 s rest, 67–85% 1RM, controlled tempo, **RIR 1–3** (not RIR 0 — this client doesn't have recovery budget for grinding sets).

Placement: Friday (after Perform Upper, lower body least loaded) or the day after Sweat Engine — never within 24–48 h of Monday/Wednesday (§7). Zero added axial or lower-body load.

Example shape: chest-supported row 4×8–10 → incline DB curl 3×10–12 → face pull/rear delt 3×12–15 → standing calf raise 3×12–15, tempo controlled, RIR 2. No barbell, no squat/hinge pattern — it doesn't touch what's already crushing them.

**2. Fix the recovery deficit before adding more — this is the actual lever for "gain size without feeling destroyed."**
Per the MODIFY ladder (§15), and because sleep/stress are the stated constraint, not the REVL program:
- Ask which of the 4 REVL sessions they're actually doing and how they feel after each (§15 "ask, don't assume"). If Sat/Sun team formats are being run at full intent rather than paced, that's often the hidden cost — both are moderate-high total-work days people mistake for "recovery" (§7).
- Consider **trading one Sweat session for the PT session** rather than stacking a 5th session on top of REVL's 4 — same weekly session count, lower total fatigue, more of the hour spent on the thing they actually want (size) instead of more capped conditioning they're not lacking.
- Autoregulate REVL itself with RIR rather than chasing the posted %/pace on weeks they're under-recovered — this is within the client's control and doesn't require leaving the program.
- Sleep: general information only, not prescriptive medical nutrition/sleep therapy *(scope, Wk01 Ch1 p7–8)* — but worth naming plainly to the client: 6 h is the more likely reason they feel destroyed than the training itself, and protecting sleep will do more for both recovery *and* hypertrophy than any exercise-selection change.

**3. Monitor and escalate.**
If "destroyed" persists beyond ~1–2 weeks after this adjustment, that's the course's threshold to reduce total load further and review sleep/stress properly rather than iterate on exercise selection *(Wk07 Ch11 p47–48)*.

**Net:** keep REVL 4×/week if they want to stay, place the PT session on horizontal pull / arms / rear delt / calves at RIR 1–3 away from Mon/Wed, and treat the "destroyed" feeling as a recovery-budget problem to fix (session trade, RIR autoregulation on REVL, sleep) rather than a training-stimulus gap to fill.

Here's how I'd work through this one, per the ISA CPT framework (ACSM screening in Ch 5, chronic-disease tables in Ch 13).

## 1. Screening — this client needs medical clearance first

Per the **ACSM preparticipation algorithm** *(Wk04 Ch5 p8)*: he **does not currently exercise**, and he has a **known metabolic disease (T2DM)** — that combination sits in the "known CV/metabolic/renal disease, regardless of symptom status" branch, which reads **medical clearance recommended**, not just "not necessary." This is a **BLOCKING** item — I wouldn't prescribe intensity/volume beyond light activity until he brings back a clearance/release, ideally with any restrictions the physician wants noted *(the sample clearance-request letter, Wk04 Ch5 p13)*.

While you have him, also run:
- **PAR-Q+** *(Wk04 Ch5 p11)* — he'll trip Q1 (HBP) and Q5 (meds), which routes to the ePARmed-X+ or physician sign-off anyway.
- **ACSM risk stratification** *(Wk04 Ch5 p14)*: age 41 doesn't score, but hypertension (+1, confirmed/on meds) counts, and check waist/BMI, family history, smoking, lipids — worth knowing his total risk-factor count even post-clearance.
- **Resting vitals** *(Ch 7)* — baseline HR and BP before session 1, and again pre/post every early session.

## 2. Medication effects you need to plan around

- **Beta blocker**: blunts both resting and exercise HR — %MHR-based prescription will be wrong. Use **RPE or the talk test**, not heart-rate zones *(Wk04 Ch5 p15–16, confirmed in programming-reference.md #10)*.
- **Metformin**: doesn't typically cause hypoglycemia on its own, but still worth doing the standard diabetes glucose checks below, especially early on while you're both learning how he responds.

## 3. Program structure

**Phase (ACE-IFT Muscular Training):** he's fully sedentary with no reported training history — start in **Functional phase** (postural stability, core, balance, kinetic-chain mobility, bodyweight/body-segment loads) rather than jumping straight to external load, per *Wk02 Ch2 p10–14*. Run a quick posture/movement screen (Ch 10) in session 1 to confirm — if he screens clean on stability, you can move into **Movement phase** (the 5 primary patterns: push, pull, bend-and-lift, single-leg, rotation) sooner than a client who screens poorly.

**FITT-VP** — starting from the Diabetes and Hypertension tables *(Wk10 Ch13 p18, p39; both override the general healthy-adult numbers)*:

| Variable | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 2 d/wk to start (both conditions' floor is 2–3 d/wk) | Ch13 p18, p39 |
| Intensity | 40–50% 1RM (novice/sedentary-beginner band) | Table 11-10 |
| Sets × reps | 1–3 × 8–12, starting at the higher-rep end (10–15) | Ch13 p39 |
| Rest | 2–3 min | Table 11-10 |
| Type | Machines/bodyweight first, all major muscle groups, multi-joint before single-joint | Table 11-10 |
| Tempo | ~6 s controlled reps (good for new exercisers) | Ch11 p17 |

**Hard constraints, both conditions** *(Ch13 p17–18, p40–41)*:
- **Avoid isometrics and inverted positions**; avoid Valsalva — coach exhale-on-exertion breathing.
- **Blood pressure**: measure pre/post session; **stop the session if SBP >250 or DBP >115, or if SBP fails to rise / drops ≥20 mmHg with increasing workload.** Prolong the cool-down (no abrupt stop → dizziness risk on the beta blocker).
- **Blood glucose** (have him self-monitor if he already does): start only if **≥100 and ≤250 mg/dL**; check every 30–60 min if the session runs long, and again after. Know the hypoglycemia symptom list and the **15-15 rule**, and keep fast-acting carbs on hand *(Ch13 p40–41)*.

## 4. First 2–4 weeks, concretely

- 2 non-consecutive days/week, full-body, Functional→Movement phase.
- 6–8 exercises: bodyweight squat-to-box or sit-to-stand, hip hinge pattern (light/assisted), push (wall/incline press), row (band or machine), a core/anti-extension drill, single-leg balance work.
- Warm-up 5–10 min light rhythmic cardio + dynamic mobility; cool-down 5–10 min with static stretching *(Ch11 p18, Ch8 p41)*.
- Progress via the **2-for-2 rule** — two consecutive sessions exceeding target reps by ≥2 on the last set before adding load, ~5% increments *(Ch11 p7, p19–20)* — deliberately slow given he's both a true beginner and has two conditions where the course explicitly says "start conservative, modify for safety."

## 5. What I'd flag as open/general-knowledge

- No BP, HbA1c/fasting glucose, or waist/BMI numbers given yet — these change how conservative to be and whether he lands in a higher risk-stratification bracket. Worth getting before session 1.
- The course doesn't give a specific cardio prescription question here since he asked about strength training specifically, but T2DM's cardio floor (≥150 min/wk moderate, Ch13 p39) is worth mentioning to him even if it's not the PT session focus — that's course-supported, just outside what you asked.

If you want, give me his name and I can turn this into a proper client file (`.md` + `.csv`) once you've got his clearance and baseline numbers back — happy to hold off until then given the BLOCKING clearance item.

Here's the read and the plan. A few upfront notes on gaps, then the programming.

## Gaps before this is locked in (ask Ivy)
- **BLOCKING – screening**: no PAR-Q+/ACSM screen on file yet *(Wk04 Ch5)*. "Trained on and off for a year" doesn't rule out risk factors — run it before adding real load, especially given the pressing focus (shoulder health matters more than most).

I'll answer the programming question now on reasonable assumptions (novice-ish trainee, no red flags, standard hotel-gym DB rack) and flag anywhere that would change if the answers come back differently.

## Why this isn't a "give them a press program" question

Two things push back on the obvious instinct to just load up pressing:

**1. REVL already trains pressing a fair amount.** Per the REVL data: BB bench press appears on ~35% of all sessions (63% of Fridays — Perform Upper — and 54% of Sundays), and overhead press/jerk on ~38% (65% Monday, 62% Sunday). Vertical push overall is 50% of sessions. Pressing is *not* one of REVL's clear gaps the way carries or rotation are. Stack a dedicated 3x/week PT press block blindly on top of that and you risk redundant pressing — the same failure mode flagged for a full Russian wave (a press wave + Friday Perform Upper + Sunday Complete = 3–4 pressing sessions/week, no room to recover).

**2. A "real" strength block (Russian protocol) doesn't fit here anyway** — Ivy is inconsistent (a year on/off, not an established, consistent lifter), which fails the experienced-lifter gate for that archetype, and there's no barbell for a month regardless. So this isn't "which Russian variant" — it's REVL-complementary accessory pressing work, done with the smallest effective dose, using what's actually available.

## What the Volume phase buys you

Good news: Volume (weeks 1–3) is REVL's highest-headroom phase — loads run ~40–65%, and per the combined-ceiling rule, PT can add **up to a normal accessory/secondary session, top-set intensity capped ~80% or RIR ≥3**. This is the best 3-week window in the block to actually move the needle on pressing, better than waiting for Build/Peak where headroom disappears.

## The travel-month plan (3x/week PT, DB/bodyweight only)

Structure around what's missing, not more of what REVL already covers:

**Session A — Pressing emphasis (place away from Friday/Sunday REVL sessions if possible)**
- DB flat bench press 4×6–10, RIR 2–3
- DB seated/standing shoulder press 3×8–10, RIR 2–3
- Horizontal pull to balance the pressing (row/inverted row) 3×10–12 — this also fills a genuine REVL gap (horizontal pull sits at ~39% overall)
- Rear-delt/scap work (band pull-apart, face pull) 2–3×12–15 — shoulder-health insurance for someone ramping pressing volume

**Session B — Complementary, not competing (lower body/trunk)**
- REVL loads the lower body on every training day (squat 73–74%, hinge 74–76% of sessions) — don't add more of that. Use this session for what REVL never gives: carries (suitcase/farmer's, 8–11% gap), anti-rotation (Pallof press), single-leg *stability* work at light load, and a short Zone 1–2 aerobic piece if Ivy lacks a base — REVL has zero true easy aerobic work.

**Session C — Pressing accessory + weak point + technique**
- Incline DB press or push-up variation (tempo, deficit, or weighted) 3–4×8–12
- Triceps/close-grip work 3×10–12
- Technique/positioning drills at light load — REVL is 100% time-capped, so this is the only place Ivy ever gets *untimed* pressing technique work, which matters more for someone with only a year of inconsistent training.

**Intensity/progression**: since there's no barbell and probably no fresh 1RM, run this by RIR/RPE and double progression rather than %1RM — add a rep each session within the range, then add load once at the top of the rep range for 2 sessions straight *(2‑for‑2 rule, Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20)*. Novice trainees respond well even to moderate volume here — no need to chase near-maximal loads *(Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10, p29–31)*.

**Scheduling rule**: don't place Session A or C within ~48h of Ivy's REVL Friday (Perform Upper) or Sunday (Complete) if avoidable — that's where REVL's own pressing volume concentrates. Once you confirm Ivy's actual REVL days, I can slot these precisely.

## Most likely cause of the regression

Raj is doing **7 total training sessions/week** (4 REVL + 3 PT) with an **inconsistent training history** (on-and-off for a year), landing in REVL's **Volume phase** — which is actually the *highest-density* phase in the programme (72% of sessions are EMOM-style, back-to-back work with short rest) even though loads are lower (40–65% 1RM). Volume phase reads as "easy" on the load axis but it's the **most metabolically/muscularly demanding phase by density** *(revl-class-integration.md §4)*.

For a client with low accumulated work capacity, stacking 3 more PT sessions on top of that is a classic setup for **non-functional overreaching**, not a skill or programming problem. Two weeks of declining numbers plus rising frequency is the pattern the course flags under recovery/overtraining — chronic performance decrement is a stop-and-reassess signal, not a "push through it" signal *(recovery & overtraining, Wk07 Ch11 p47–48)*. This is a course-supported read, but I'm inferring it's the driver here rather than confirming it — I don't have Raj's sleep, life stress, or actual RIR/loads used in REVL yet.

**Before changing the program, screen this properly** (BLOCKING before I'd write real prescriptions):
- Sleep quantity/quality and life stress over the last 2 weeks
- Which REVL sessions Raj actually attended and at what RIR (self-selected load in a class setting varies a lot)
- Any joint pain/soreness that isn't resolving between sessions
- Appetite/energy trends, any illness
- PAR-Q+/ACSM screen if not already done — REVL attendance isn't medical clearance *(Wk04 Ch5)*

If any of those flag something beyond normal fatigue (persistent pain, resolved-then-recurring symptoms), that's a referral-out trigger, not a programming fix.

## What to do with the PT sessions right now

Two moves, both course-supported:

Cut total volume before doing anything else.** Per the modify-in-order rule *(revl-class-integration.md §15)*: drop intensity → drop volume → swap to lower-demand variants → change session type entirely. Here's how I'd approach Freya's PT session, working from the REVL integration framework plus the core ISA CPT principles.

## First, name what's actually going on

Three things point the same direction:

1. **REVL Volume phase's own stated intent is "accumulate work capacity + muscle"** — that's already the stimulus Freya is getting 4x/week, at high density (72% EMOM-style) and mostly partner/team format (80%) *[Observed, revl-class-integration.md §4]*. If the PT session just adds more of the same, it's not filling a gap — it's stacking on an already-saturated stimulus, and this is Volume week 1-3 not week 1 of nothing.
2. **They're 8 years in and near their ceiling.** At this stage, capacity gains come from quality, specificity, and full recovery expression — not from finding one more way to fatigue the same systems. Diminishing returns on "more" are real here.
3. **Heavy work stress right now reduces their actual recovery capacity**, even though REVL's training load hasn't changed. The course frames periodization's benefit as protecting *planned physical and mental recovery* (Week 07, Ch 11 p42) — mental/life stress counts against that budget, not just training stress.

So the highest-value PT session this week is the smallest, most complementary dose — not a second capacity session.

## What REVL Volume phase is *not* giving Freya

From the REVL gap analysis (§6a, both years of captured data):
- **True Zone 1-2 aerobic work — 0% of sessions.** Everything at REVL is capped/competitive. If "work capacity" means aerobic base, this is the actual missing piece, and it's low-interference (won't compound soreness or add axial/lower-body load).
- **Carries/loaded holds — 8-11%.** Cheap, low-fatigue-cost, genuinely builds capacity.
- **Horizontal pulling — 28-39%,** concentrated on just two days.
- **Rotation/anti-rotation** — condition this on which Wednesday shape Freya actually does (Move Total = gap; Move Upper = already served). Worth a 30-second question before programming it.
- **Technique/movement quality at sub-maximal load** — REVL is 100% time-capped, so nothing untimed or quality-focused exists anywhere in their week.

## Session shape I'd run

Assuming a Perform/Move split where the PT day lands after their upper-emphasis or lightest lower-body day (ask which — don't assume):

1. **Warm-up** scaled to what they've already carried that week, not a fresh-body warm-up.
2. **Zone 1-2 aerobic piece**, 20-30 min, talk-test pace — the one thing REVL structurally cannot deliver, and it directly serves "work capacity" without adding fatigue debt during a stressful period.
3. **Carries** (suitcase or offset, 3-4 sets) — capacity + trunk, negligible soreness.
4. **Horizontal row, controlled tempo**, moderate reps — fills the pulling gap.
5. **Anti-rotation work** — only if Freya's Wednesday is Move Total; skip if Move Upper.
6. **RIR ≥ 3 throughout, no near-maximal work.** Volume phase has headroom, but "headroom" assumes normal recovery capacity — the work-stress context means I'd program to the conservative end of that headroom, not the top.
7. **Close with brief downregulation/breathing** — cheap, directly counters the allostatic load from work stress, and reframes the session's "win" as something other than fatigue.

## The soreness belief

This is worth addressing directly and early, because it will otherwise sabotage the whole plan above — Freya will read a session with no DOMS as "wasted" and either push it harder than programmed or lose confidence in it.

Flagging clearly: **the course doesn't explicitly cover DOMS mechanics, so what follows is general exercise-science knowledge, not a course citation.** What I'd tell Freya:

- Soreness reflects unaccustomed or eccentric-heavy stress, not the completeness or quality of a training stimulus. An 8-year lifter doing well-grooved patterns will often *not* be sore from effective work — that's adaptation, not failure.
- Chasing soreness as the success metric, especially while already under-recovering from work stress, pushes toward exactly the failure mode periodization exists to prevent (Ch 11 p42's "reduced risk of overtraining" is explicitly about protecting recovery, not maximizing damage).
- Reframe the win: performance markers this session (did the aerobic piece feel controlled at the target pace, was carry form solid unbroken, did rowing tempo stay honest) rather than next-day muscle pain. This is a straightforward application of self-efficacy/belief work from Ch 3 — you're not fighting the belief, you're giving her a better one to replace it with, backed by what she can actually observe in-session.
- Practically: I'd literally have her rate the session 1-10 on "did I hit the intended quality" rather than ask "are you sore tomorrow" — get the conversation off soreness as the proxy.

One thing I'd want before finalizing: confirm whether she's on Perform or Move, and if Move, which Wednesday shape (Move Total vs Move Upper) — that changes whether anti-rotation work is a real gap or already covered. Want me to turn this into a tracked client file so we can log her actual sessions and adjust week to week, or is this a one-off session plan?
